claim: The low-complexity domain of hnRNPA1 (A1-LCD) phase separates in a salt-dependent manner.
source: The low-complexity domain of hnRNPA1 (A1-LCD) phase separates in a salt-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a general statement about A1-LCD behavior that is supported by the experimental data and simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Unlike many intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) whose phase separation is suppressed by increasing salt concentrations, the phase separation of A1-LCD is promoted by >100 mM NaCl.
source: Unlike many intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) whose phase separation is suppressed by increasing salt concentrations, the phase separation of A1-LCD is promoted by >100 mM NaCl.
evidence: This claim contrasts A1-LCD behavior with typical IDP behavior and is supported by experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ions occupy first shell as well as more distant sites around the IDP chains.
source: The ions occupy first shell as well as more distant sites around the IDP chains, with Arg sidechains and backbone carbonyls the favored partners of Cl– and Na+, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MD simulation data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Arg sidechains are the favored partners of Cl– ions.
source: The ions occupy first shell as well as more distant sites around the IDP chains, with Arg sidechains and backbone carbonyls the favored partners of Cl– and Na+, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by RDF calculations showing strong peaks for Cl– around Arg sidechains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Backbone carbonyls are the favored partners of Na+ ions.
source: The ions occupy first shell as well as more distant sites around the IDP chains, with Arg sidechains and backbone carbonyls the favored partners of Cl– and Na+, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by RDF calculations and ion coordination analysis showing that backbone oxygens coordinate the largest number of Na+ ions (Figure 3A).

claim: Ions neutralize the high net charge of A1-LCD (+9) by an excess of bound Cl– over Na+.
source: The first is to neutralize the high net charge of the protein (+9) by an excess of bound Cl– over Na+
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3B and 3C showing excess Cl– binding and net charge reduction.

claim: Ions bridge between A1-LCD chains, thereby fortifying the intermolecular interaction networks in the dense phase.
source: the second is to bridge between A1-LCD chains, thereby fortifying the intermolecular interaction networks in the dense phase.
evidence: This is supported by the bridging ion analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: At high concentrations, NaCl indirectly strengthens π–π, cation–π, and amino–π interactions by drawing water away from the interaction partners.
source: At high concentrations, NaCl also indirectly strengthens π–π, cation–π, and amino–π interactions, by drawing water away from the interaction partners.
evidence: This is supported by RDF calculations showing decreased water density around interaction partners at high salt (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: At low salt, A1-LCD is prevented from phase separation by net charge repulsion.
source: Therefore, at low salt, A1-LCD is prevented from phase separation by net charge repulsion
evidence: This is supported by simulation data showing lack of condensation at 50 mM NaCl (Figure 1C, Figure 2A) and the high net charge at low salt (Figure 3C).

claim: At intermediate concentrations, NaCl neutralizes enough of the net charge while also bridging IDP chains to drive phase separation.
source: at intermediate concentrations, NaCl neutralizes enough of the net charge while also bridging IDP chains to drive phase separation.
evidence: This is supported by the progressive reduction in net charge (Figure 3C) and increase in bridging ions (Figure 4B) at intermediate salt concentrations.

claim: The drive for phase separation becomes even stronger at high salt due to strengthened π-type interactions.
source: This drive becomes even stronger at high salt due to strengthened π-type interactions.
evidence: This is supported by the increased number of π-type interactions at high salt (Figure 5A) and water withdrawal from interaction partners (Figure 5E).

claim: Four classes of salt dependence of IDP phase separation can be predicted from amino-acid composition.
source: Based on this understanding, four classes of salt dependence of IDP phase separation can be predicted from amino-acid composition.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figure 6C and Table 1 showing correlations between amino acid composition and salt dependence class.

claim: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) mediate a variety of cellular functions such as biogenesis of the ribosome and stress response.
source: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) mediate a variety of cellular functions such as biogenesis of the ribosome and stress response (Mitrea et al., 2018; Protter and Parker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The driver for phase separation or condensation is intermolecular interactions, including electrostatic, hydrogen bonding, π–π, cation–π, amino–π, and hydrophobic.
source: The driver for phase separation or condensation is intermolecular interactions, including electrostatic, hydrogen bonding, π–π, cation–π, amino–π, and hydrophobic (Das et al., 2020; Dignon et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: High salt strengthens hydrophobic interactions by increasing the surface tension of water.
source: In particular, high salt strengthens hydrophobic interactions by increasing the surface tension of water (Baldwin, 1996; Zhou and Pang, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The most typical effect of salt is the suppression of phase separation by screening electrostatic attraction, both for homotypic systems and for heterotypic systems.
source: The most typical effect is the suppression of phase separation by screening electrostatic attraction, both for homotypic systems (Berry et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Brady et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2017; Reed and Hammer, 2018; Tsang et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024) and for heterotypic systems (Farag et al., 2023; Galvanetto et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Salt can also promote phase separation, although the mechanism is not always clear.
source: However, salt can also promote phase separation, although the mechanism is not always clear (Martin et al., 2021; Muschol and Rosenberger, 1997; Burke et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Dao et al., 2018; Babinchak et al., 2019; Le Ferrand et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2021; Krainer et al., 2021; Otis and Sharpe, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: Krainer et al., 2021 observed a 'reentrant' salt effect on the phase separation of five intrinsically disordered proteins: phase separation occurs without salt, is prohibited by medium salt, and reemerges at high salt.
source: In particular, Krainer et al., 2021 observed a 'reentrant' salt effect on the phase separation of five intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs): phase separation occurs without salt, is prohibited by medium salt, and reemerges at high salt.
evidence: This is a direct citation of findings from Krainer et al., 2021.

claim: Krainer et al., 2021 attributed the reemergence of phase separation to strengthened π-type and hydrophobic interactions that overcompensate weakened electrostatic attraction.
source: They attributed the reemergence of phase separation to strengthened π-type and hydrophobic interactions that overcompensate weakened electrostatic attraction.
evidence: This is a citation of the interpretation from Krainer et al., 2021.

claim: The full-length hnRNPA1 protein, comprising folded domains along with the LCD, phase separates in the absence of salt and the tendency to phase separate is reduced upon adding salt.
source: The full-length protein, comprising folded domains along with the LCD, phase separates in the absence of salt and the tendency to phase separate is reduced upon adding salt, thus exhibiting the typical salt effect.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: A screening mechanism, specifically of electrostatic attraction between the LCD and the folded domains, is supported by small-angle X-ray scattering and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations for full-length hnRNPA1.
source: A screening mechanism, specifically of electrostatic attraction between the LCD and the folded domains, is supported by small-angle X-ray scattering and coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: A1-LCD does not phase separate without salt and starts to do so only after 100 mM NaCl is added.
source: In contrast, A1-LCD does not phase separate without salt and starts to do so only after 100 mM NaCl is added.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: π-types of interactions, mediated by aromatic residues, drive the phase separation of A1-LCD.
source: An earlier study revealed that π-types of interactions, mediated by aromatic residues, drive the phase separation of A1-LCD (Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2020.

claim: The net charge plays a strong suppressive role in A1-LCD phase separation.
source: A follow-up study, based on charge mutations, further showed that the net charge plays a strong suppressive role (Bremer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bremer et al., 2022.

claim: The saturation concentration (Csat) for A1-LCD phase separation is minimum at a net charge near 0.
source: The saturation concentration (Csat) for phase separation is minimum at a net charge near 0, and increases by two orders of magnitude, signifying an enormous weakening of the drive for phase separation, when the net charge moves away from neutrality in either direction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bremer et al., 2022.

claim: Csat for A1-LCD increases by two orders of magnitude when the net charge moves away from neutrality in either direction.
source: The saturation concentration (Csat) for phase separation is minimum at a net charge near 0, and increases by two orders of magnitude, signifying an enormous weakening of the drive for phase separation, when the net charge moves away from neutrality in either direction.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bremer et al., 2022.

claim: Salt promoted the homotypic phase separation of both A1-LCD and FUS-LCD, but suppressed the heterotypic phase separation of their mixture.
source: In a more recent study, salt promoted the homotypic phase separation of both A1-LCD and FUS-LCD, but suppressed the heterotypic phase separation of their mixture (Farag et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Farag et al., 2023.

claim: All-atom MD simulations can uniquely provide mechanistic insight into the driving force and properties of biomolecular condensates.
source: All-atom MD simulations can uniquely provide mechanistic insight into the driving force and properties of biomolecular condensates (Zhou et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2024 and is a general statement about the capabilities of all-atom MD simulations.

claim: ATP, a small molecule with a −4 charge, bridges between positively charged IDP chains in driving phase separation.
source: For example, these simulations showed that ATP, a small molecule with a −4 charge, bridges between positively charged IDP chains in driving phase separation (Kota et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kota et al., 2024.

claim: The intermolecular interactions in condensates quickly break and reform, explaining why the condensates can rapidly fuse despite very high macroscopic viscosity.
source: The intermolecular interactions quickly break and reform, explaining why the condensates can rapidly fuse despite very high macroscopic viscosity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kota et al., 2024.

claim: Quick breakup and reformation of salt bridges in a heterotypic condensate allow the protein molecules to be extremely dynamic in a highly viscous environment.
source: Similarly, quick breakup and reformation of salt bridges in a heterotypic condensate allow the protein molecules to be extremely dynamic in a highly viscous environment (Galvanetto et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galvanetto et al., 2023.

claim: All attractive residue–residue contacts contribute to the drive for phase separation.
source: These and other simulations (Rekhi et al., 2024) show that all attractive residue–residue contacts contribute to the drive for phase separation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2024 and Rekhi et al., 2024.

claim: The 131-residue A1-LCD is comprised mostly of Gly and Ser (51 and 22, respectively), followed by 18 aromatic residues (11 Phe and 7 Tyr), 17 residues with sidechain amides (13 Asn and 4 Gln), and 15 charged residues (10 Arg, 2 Lys, and 3 Asp), with a large net charge of +9.
source: The 131-residue A1-LCD is comprised mostly of Gly and Ser (51 and 22, respectively), followed by 18 aromatic residues (11 Phe and 7 Tyr), 17 residues with sidechain amides (13 Asn and 4 Gln), and 15 charged residues (10 Arg, 2 Lys, and 3 Asp), with a large net charge of +9 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: An 8-copy model for the dense phase was built with an initial concentration of 3.5 mM at five NaCl concentrations ranging from 50 to 1000 mM.
source: we built an 8-copy model for the dense phase (with an initial concentration of 3.5 mM) at five NaCl concentrations ranging from 50 to 1000 mM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the simulation setup.

claim: The initial concentration of 3.5 mM is close to the measured concentration at the critical point.
source: This initial concentration is close to the measured concentration at the critical point (Martin et al., 2020), thereby facilitating the comparison between low salt (where phase separation does not occur) and high salt (where phase separation does occur).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2020.

claim: Each system was simulated in four replicates for 1.5 μs each.
source: Each system was simulated in four replicates for 1.5 μs each.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol.

claim: From the same initial configuration with very few inter-chain contacts, the systems maintain the initial loose configuration at 50 mM NaCl but condense noticeably at 1000 mM NaCl.
source: From the same initial configuration with very few inter-chain contacts, the systems maintain the initial loose configuration at 50 mM NaCl (Figure 1C) but condense noticeably at 1000 mM NaCl (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the simulation snapshots shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: At low salt, the protein chains have a tendency to fill the simulation box, occasionally spanning the entire box in one or two of the three orthogonal directions.
source: At low salt, the protein chains have a tendency to fill the simulation box, occasionally spanning the entire box in one or two of the three orthogonal directions and exhibiting larger-scale reconfiguration based on root-mean-square-fluctuation (RMSF) calculation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and quantified by RMSF calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: At high salt, the chains aggregate into an ellipsoidal particle, with the RMSF reduced by 27%.
source: In contrast, at high salt, the chains aggregate into an ellipsoidal particle, with the RMSF reduced by 27%.
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and quantified by RMSF calculations.

claim: The Dmax values are close to the initial value (~150 Å) at low salt (50 mM NaCl), but decrease to ~135 Å at intermediate salt (150 and 300 mM NaCl) and further to ~120 Å at high salt (500 and 1000 mM NaCl).
source: The Dmax values are close to the initial value (~150 Å) at low salt (50 mM NaCl), but decrease to ~135 Å at intermediate salt (150 and 300 mM NaCl) and further to ~120 Å at high salt (500 and 1000 mM NaCl; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The systems show a lack of condensation at low salt, and growing condensation on going to intermediate and high salt.
source: Overall, the systems show a lack of condensation at low salt, and growing condensation on going to intermediate and high salt.
evidence: This is inferred from the Dmax measurements and visual inspection of simulation snapshots.

claim: The concentration of the condensed particle is estimated to be 23 mM, which is similar to the measured concentration in the dense phase.
source: Modeling the condensed particle as an ellipsoid with the principal diameters given by the maximum dimensions in the three orthogonal directions, we can estimate its concentration to be 23 mM, which is similar to the measured concentration in the dense phase (Martin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation data and compared to experimental measurements from Martin et al., 2020.

claim: The average radius of gyration (Rg) shows a decreasing trend with increasing salt.
source: The average radius of gyration (Rg) shows a decreasing trend with increasing salt (Figure 2B), which matches the experimental data (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations (Figure 2B) and compared to experimental data from Martin et al., 2021.

claim: The average number of intrachain contacts per residue increases slightly, by 5%, when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM.
source: Correspondingly, the average number of intrachain contacts per residue increases slightly, by 5%, when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The number of inter-chain contacts per residue increases by 23% when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM.
source: However, the main driver of the condensation is inter-chain interactions, with inter-chain contacts per residue increasing by 23% over the same salt range.
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: High salt induces A1-LCD condensation, with an increased number of interactions between protein chains.
source: Clearly, high salt induces A1-LCD condensation, with an increased number of interactions between protein chains.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on Dmax, Rg, and inter-chain contacts.

claim: At 1000 mM NaCl, the RDFs of Cl– show a strong 1st peak at 3.2 Å around Arg and Lys sidechain nitrogens.
source: At 1000 mM NaCl, the RDFs of Cl– show a strong 1st peak at 3.2 Å around Arg and Lys sidechain nitrogens and a moderate 1st peak around the Gln and Asn sidechain nitrogens and the Ser sidechain oxygen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each Arg sidechain often coordinates two Cl– ions simultaneously, but each Lys sidechain coordinates only one Cl– ion.
source: Each Arg sidechain often coordinates two Cl– ions simultaneously, but each Lys sidechain coordinates only one Cl– ion.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation trajectories.

claim: A 2nd peak, at ~5 Å, is observed in the Cl– RDF around Arg and Lys sidechain nitrogens.
source: A 2nd peak, at ~5 Å, is also observed around Arg and Lys sidechain nitrogens.
evidence: This is measured from the RDF calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cutoffs of 4 and 6.4 Å were used to define 1st- and 2nd-shell Cl– binding, respectively.
source: We used cutoffs of 4 and 6.4 Å, respectively, to define 1st- and 2nd-shell Cl– binding.
evidence: This describes the analysis methodology.

claim: On a per-residue basis, Arg and Lys sidechains coordinate the most 1st-shell Cl– ions, reaching ~0.25 ions per residue.
source: On a per-residue basis, Arg and Lys sidechains coordinate the most 1st-shell Cl– ions, reaching ~0.25 ions per residue (Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Arg and Ser residues coordinate the most 1st-shell Cl– ions, 21.5 and 8.4, respectively, in the 8-chain system at 1000 mM NaCl.
source: Given the large numbers of Arg and Ser residues in the A1-LCD sequence, these two residue types coordinate the most 1st-shell Cl– ions, 21.5 and 8.4, respectively, in the 8-chain system at 1000 mM NaCl.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: Backbone nitrogens coordinate 13.4, or the second most 1st-shell Cl– ions at 1000 mM NaCl.
source: Although the RDF around backbone nitrogens has only a weak 1st peak, given their large number (131 per chain), they actually coordinate 13.4, or the second most 1st-shell Cl– ions.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: Among the 13.4 Cl– ions coordinated with backbone nitrogens, 55% are coordinated with Gly residues.
source: Among these 13.4 Cl– ions, 55% are coordinated with Gly residues.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: Gly is favored for Cl– coordination due to its lack of sidechain, which allows the close approach of ions to the backbone.
source: A large part of this high percentage is due to the enrichment of Gly (39% of all residues) in the A1-LCD sequence, but Gly is additionally favored for its lack of sidechain, which allows the close approach of ions to the backbone.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural properties of Gly and the simulation data.

claim: Na+ shows a very strong preference for the Asp carboxyl in 1st-shell coordination, with a peak RDF value of 9.2 at 2.2 Å.
source: Na+ shows a very strong preference for the Asp carboxyl in 1st-shell coordination, with a peak RDF value of 9.2 at 2.2 Å (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Each Asp sidechain carboxyl typically coordinates a single Na+ ion, usually in a bifurcated geometry.
source: Each Asp sidechain carboxyl typically coordinates a single Na+ ion, usually in a bifurcated geometry.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation trajectories.

claim: Na+ shows a strong preference in 1st-shell coordination with Asn and Gln sidechain amide oxygens and the backbone carbonyl oxygen as well as a moderate preference with the Ser sidechain oxygen.
source: In addition, Na+ shows a strong preference in 1st-shell coordination with Asn and Gln sidechain amide oxygens and the backbone carbonyl oxygen as well as a moderate preference with the Ser sidechain oxygen.
evidence: This is measured from the RDF calculations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Cutoffs of 3 and 5.4 Å were used to define 1st- and 2nd-shell Na+ binding, respectively.
source: We used cutoffs of 3 and 5.4 Å, respectively, to define 1st- and 2nd-shell Na+ binding.
evidence: This describes the analysis methodology.

claim: On a per-residue basis, the Asp sidechain coordinates the most 1st-shell Na+ ions, reaching 0.17 ions per residue.
source: On a per-residue basis, the Asp sidechain coordinates the most 1st-shell Na+ ions, reaching 0.17 ions per residue (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Backbone oxygens coordinate 27.9 1st-shell Na+ ions in the 8-chain system at 1000 mM NaCl.
source: Again, due to their large number, backbone oxygens coordinate a very large number, 27.9, of 1st-shell Na+ in the 8-chain system at 1000 mM NaCl.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: The largest number of 1st-shell Cl– ions are coordinated with Arg sidechains but the largest number of 1st-shell Na+ ions are coordinated with backbone carbonyls.
source: Overall, the largest number of 1st-shell Cl– ions are coordinated with Arg sidechains but the largest number of 1st-shell Na+ ions are coordinated with backbone carbonyls.
evidence: This is summarized from the ion coordination analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Multiple backbone carbonyls often coordinate a single Na+ ion, with at least two backbone carbonyl partners for 30.6 of the 64.1 bound Na+ ions (1st- and 2nd-shell).
source: Whereas each Arg sidechain often coordinates two Cl– ions, multiple backbone carbonyls often coordinate a single Na+ ion, with at least two backbone carbonyl partners for 30.6 of the 64.1 bound Na+ ions (1st- and 2nd-shell).
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: Both the 1st-shell Cl– and Na+ ions increase with increasing NaCl concentration, and Cl– ions always outnumber Na+ ions.
source: Both the 1st-shell Cl– and Na+ ions increase with increasing NaCl concentration, and Cl– ions always outnumber Na+ ions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The difference between 1st-shell Cl– and Na+ ions remains almost constant, with around 10 more 1st-shell Cl– ions than 1st-shell Na+ ions.
source: The difference remains almost constant, with around 10 more 1st-shell Cl– ions than 1st-shell Na+ ions.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3B.

claim: The difference of 10 more 1st-shell Cl– ions than Na+ ions is not enough to neutralize the total charge, +72, on the protein chains.
source: This difference is not enough to neutralize the total charge, +72, on the protein chains.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the ion excess to the total protein charge.

claim: When 2nd-shell ions are included, the excess of bound Cl– ions over bound Na+ ions grows quickly with increasing NaCl concentration.
source: However, when 2nd-shell ions are also included, the excess of bound Cl– ions over bound Na+ ions grows quickly with increasing NaCl concentration.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The net charge of the system reduces to zero at 1000 mM NaCl when 1st- and 2nd-shell ions are included.
source: Correspondingly, the net charge of the system reduces to zero at 1000 mM NaCl (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Net charge repulsion explains why the chains maintain their initial loose configuration in the simulations at 50 mM NaCl and the observed absence of phase separation at this low salt concentration.
source: Net charge repulsion explains why the chains maintain their initial loose configuration in the simulations at 50 mM NaCl (Figure 1C) and the observed absence of phase separation at this low salt concentration (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data and experimental observations.

claim: At high salt, the protein net charge is completely neutralized by 1st- and 2nd-shell ions; hence the protein chains condense and phase separation was readily observed.
source: At high salt, the protein net charge is completely neutralized by 1st- and 2nd-shell ions; hence the protein chains condense (Figure 1D) and phase separation was readily observed (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing charge neutralization and condensation, and experimental observations of phase separation.

claim: Cl– has a tendency to bind with Arg and other sidechains from multiple chains.
source: Indeed, we found that Cl– has a tendency to bind with Arg and other sidechains from multiple chains and likewise, Na+ has a tendency to bind with backbone carbonyls and sidechain oxygens from multiple chains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation trajectories and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Na+ has a tendency to bind with backbone carbonyls and sidechain oxygens from multiple chains.
source: Indeed, we found that Cl– has a tendency to bind with Arg and other sidechains from multiple chains and likewise, Na+ has a tendency to bind with backbone carbonyls and sidechain oxygens from multiple chains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation trajectories and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Close to 20% of all 1st- and 2nd-shell ions bridge between A1-LCD chains.
source: Close to 20% of all 1st- and 2nd-shell ions bridge between A1-LCD chains.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For both Cl– and Na+, the average number of bridging ions increases with increasing salt.
source: For both Cl– and Na+, the average number of bridging ions increases with increasing salt, but the pace of increase is much greater for Na+ than for Cl–, commensurate with the trend shown by the total number of bound ions of each type (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The number of bridging ions is 4.7 for Cl– and only 0.5 for Na+ in the 8-chain system at 50 mM NaCl, and increases to 26.6 and 10.9, respectively, at 1000 mM NaCl.
source: The number of bridging ions is 4.7 for Cl– and only 0.5 for Na+ in the 8-chain system at 50 mM NaCl, and increases to 26.6 and 10.9, respectively, at 1000 mM NaCl.
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The fold change of bridging Na+ ions is 23-fold, versus 6-fold for Cl–.
source: The greater fold change of bridging Na+ ions (23-fold, vs 6-fold for Cl–) is also apparent when we break the bridging ions according to the number of A1-LCD chains being bridged (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Figure 4B and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cl– strongly prefers Arg sidechains and, even at low salt, occupies a large number of sites lined by them, of which ~20% are bridging sites.
source: Cl– strongly prefers Arg sidechains and, even at low salt, occupies a large number of sites lined by them, of which ~20% are bridging sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the RDF data and bridging ion analysis.

claim: There is a relatively limited supply of Arg sidechains (a total of 80 in the 8-chain system) and hence the fold change in bridging Cl– ions upon salt increase is somewhat tempered.
source: However, there is a relatively limited supply of Arg sidechains (a total of 80 in the 8-chain system) and hence the fold change in bridging Cl– ions upon salt increase is somewhat tempered.
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid composition and the bridging ion data.

claim: Although Na+ prefers Asp sidechains, there are very few of those in the system; instead, Na+ predominantly binds to backbone carbonyls.
source: In contrast, although Na+ prefers Asp sidechains, there are very few of those in the system; instead, Na+ predominantly binds to backbone carbonyls.
evidence: This is inferred from the RDF data and ion coordination analysis.

claim: Since there is a large supply of backbone carbonyls (a total of 1048 in the 8-chain system), at high salt, Na+ ions bind to a portion of these backbone carbonyls and bridge A1-LCD chains.
source: However, since there is a large supply of backbone carbonyls (a total of 1048 in the 8-chain system), at high salt, Na+ ions bind to a portion of these backbone carbonyls and bridge A1-LCD chains.
evidence: This is inferred from the amino acid composition and the bridging ion data.

claim: Of the total 10.9 Na+ bridging ions at 1000 mM NaCl, 6.4 do so through backbone carbonyls of at least two chains.
source: Of the total 10.9 Na+ bridging ions, 6.4 do so through backbone carbonyls of at least two chains.
evidence: This is calculated from the simulation data.

claim: At low salt, chain bridging is dominated by Cl– (Na+ only 9% of bridging ions).
source: Consequently, at low salt, chain bridging is dominated by Cl– (Na+ only 9% of bridging ions), but at high salt, Na+ becomes more even (30% of bridging ions) with Cl– in bridging A1-LCD chains.
evidence: This is calculated from the bridging ion data in Figure 4B.

claim: At high salt, Na+ becomes more even (30% of bridging ions) with Cl– in bridging A1-LCD chains.
source: Consequently, at low salt, chain bridging is dominated by Cl– (Na+ only 9% of bridging ions), but at high salt, Na+ becomes more even (30% of bridging ions) with Cl– in bridging A1-LCD chains.
evidence: This is calculated from the bridging ion data in Figure 4B.

claim: An important reason for Na+ becoming more even with Cl– in bridging at high salt is Na+ coordination by backbone carbonyls, especially those of Gly residues.
source: An important reason for the latter is Na+ coordination by backbone carbonyls, especially those of Gly residues (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the ion coordination analysis and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The number of inter-chain interactions increases by 23% when the NaCl concentration increases from 50 mM to 1000 mM.
source: As noted above, the number of inter-chain interactions increases by 23% when the NaCl concentration increases from 50 mM to 1000 mM.
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: When the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM, the number of salt bridges per chain remains nearly constant, while the numbers of cation-π, π-π, and amino-π interactions increase by 17%, 26%, and 39%, respectively.
source: A breakdown of inter-chain sidechain interactions into different types reveals that when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM, the number of salt bridges per chain remains nearly constant, while the numbers of cation-π, π-π, and amino-π interactions increase by 17%, 26%, and 39%, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: As A1-LCD is condensed at high salt, there is an overall increase in inter-chain interactions, but this increase is limited to π-types of interactions and excludes salt bridges.
source: That is, as A1-LCD is condensed at high salt, there is an overall increase in inter-chain interactions, but this increase is limited to π-types of interactions and excludes salt bridges.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 5A.

claim: At increasing salt, more π-types of interactions are formed while no new salt bridges are formed, suggesting a strengthening of the former interactions.
source: At increasing salt, more π-types of interactions are formed while no new salt bridges are formed, suggesting a strengthening of the former interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 5A.

claim: The apparent null effect of salt on salt bridge formation can be attributed to the canceling of two opposing effects: chain condensation may potentially strengthen salt bridges but competition of ions with the salt-bridge partners for coordination may potentially weaken salt bridges.
source: The apparent null effect of salt on salt bridge formation can be attributed to the canceling of two opposing effects: chain condensation by the direct effects of salt may potentially shorten the distances between salt-bridge partners and thereby strengthen salt bridges but competition of ions with the salt-bridge partners for coordination (Figure 3—figure supplements 1A and 2A) may potentially weaken salt bridges.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data and structural analysis.

claim: At 1000 mM NaCl, cationic and anionic partners in a salt bridge are often found to also coordinate Cl– and Na+, respectively.
source: Indeed, at 1000 mM NaCl, cationic and anionic partners in a salt bridge are often found to also coordinate Cl– and Na+, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation trajectories and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: One partner in cation–π interactions and both partners in π–π and amino–π interactions have limited abilities to coordinate with ions, so the effects from ion competition are tempered.
source: In comparison, one partner in cation–π interactions and both partners in π–π and amino–π interactions have limited abilities to coordinate with ions, so the effects from ion competition are tempered.
evidence: This is inferred from the RDF data and structural properties of the interaction partners.

claim: For π-types of interactions, salt may exert a strengthening effect by drawing water away from the interaction partners.
source: For π-types of interactions, instead of a weakening mechanism through ion competition, salt may exert a strengthening effect by drawing water away from the interaction partners (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the water RDF data and illustrated schematically in Figure 5D.

claim: RDFs of water around Tyr sidechains that form π-types of interactions show decreases in water density when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM.
source: We calculated the RDFs of water around Tyr sidechains that form π-types of interactions and found decreases in water density when the salt concentration is increased from 50 to 1000 mM (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The decreases in water density follow the order cation–π < π–π < amino–π, which is the same order as the corresponding increases in these three types of interactions.
source: The decreases in water density follow the order cation–π < π–π < amino–π, which is the same order as the corresponding increases in these three types of interactions.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the water RDF data (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) with the interaction count data (Figure 5A).

claim: No decrease in water density is seen around Asp sidechains that form salt bridges.
source: As a control, no decrease in water density is seen around Asp sidechains that form salt bridges (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is measured from the simulations and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Water can interfere with and weaken π-types of interactions.
source: Water can interfere with and weaken π-types of interactions; by drawing water away from the interaction partners, high salt strengthens these interactions and thereby indirectly contributes to condensation.
evidence: This is inferred from the water RDF data and is consistent with general knowledge about hydration effects on interactions.

claim: By drawing water away from the interaction partners, high salt strengthens π-types of interactions and thereby indirectly contributes to condensation.
source: Water can interfere with and weaken π-types of interactions; by drawing water away from the interaction partners, high salt strengthens these interactions and thereby indirectly contributes to condensation.
evidence: This is inferred from the water RDF data and the increase in π-type interactions at high salt.

claim: The withdrawal of water from π-types of interaction partners in FUS-LCD condensates has been directly demonstrated by Raman spectroscopy.
source: Recently the withdrawal of water from π-types of interaction partners in FUS-LCD condensates has been directly demonstrated by Raman spectroscopy (Joshi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2024.

claim: NaCl has both direct and indirect effects in driving A1-LCD phase separation.
source: We have shown in atomistic detail the actions of ions in the condensation of A1-LCD over a wide range of NaCl concentrations. The MD simulations reveal that NaCl has both direct and indirect effects in driving phase separation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the simulation data presented throughout the Results section.

claim: The first direct effect of NaCl is to neutralize the net charge of A1-LCD and thereby attenuate net charge repulsion.
source: The first direct effect is to neutralize the net charge of A1-LCD and thereby attenuate net charge repulsion.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The second direct effect of NaCl is to bridge between protein chains and thereby fortify intermolecular interaction networks.
source: The second direct effect is to bridge between protein chains and thereby fortify intermolecular interaction networks.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: High salt strengthens π-types of interactions by drawing water away from the interaction partners, thereby also indirectly driving phase separation.
source: In addition, high salt strengthens π-types of interactions by drawing water away from the interaction partners, thereby also indirectly driving phase separation.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Phase separation of A1-LCD is prevented by net charge repulsion at low salt.
source: The net result is that, while phase separation of A1-LCD is prevented by net charge repulsion at low salt, it is enabled at intermediate salt through charge neutralization and chain bridging by ions.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing high net charge and lack of condensation at low salt.

claim: Phase separation of A1-LCD is enabled at intermediate salt through charge neutralization and chain bridging by ions.
source: The net result is that, while phase separation of A1-LCD is prevented by net charge repulsion at low salt, it is enabled at intermediate salt through charge neutralization and chain bridging by ions.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing partial charge neutralization, bridging ions, and condensation at intermediate salt.

claim: The drive for A1-LCD phase separation becomes even stronger at high salt, where π-types of interactions are strengthened.
source: The drive for phase separation becomes even stronger at high salt, where π-types of interactions are strengthened.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing increased π-type interactions and stronger condensation at high salt.

claim: High net charge is a suppressive factor for phase separation, as highlighted by the strong effect of A1-LCD charge mutations on Csat.
source: That high net charge is a suppressive factor is highlighted by the strong effect of A1-LCD charge mutations on Csat (Bremer et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bremer et al., 2022.

claim: The suppressive action of high net charge can be countered by the addition of salt, which exerts both direct and indirect effects.
source: Here, we have shown that this suppressive action can be countered by the addition of salt, which exerts both direct and indirect effects.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the simulation data.

claim: One direct effect of salt, neutralization of net charge, can be treated by a Debye–Hückel potential in coarse-grained simulations.
source: One of these direct effects, that is, neutralization of net charge, can be treated by a Debye–Hückel potential in coarse-grained simulations (Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tesei and Lindorff-Larsen, 2022.

claim: All-atom explicit-solvent simulations have revealed an additional direct effect (bridging between protein chains) and an indirect effect (strengthening of π-type interactions).
source: However, our all-atom explicit-solvent simulations have revealed not only an additional direct effect, that is, bridging between protein chains, but also an indirect effect, that is, strengthening of π-type interactions.
evidence: This is the main contribution of the current study, supported by the simulation data.

claim: In lattice Monte Carlo simulations of charged homopolymer chains plus counterions, counterions were found to occupy sites between chains and produce effective chain–chain attraction.
source: In lattice Monte Carlo simulations of a system of charged homopolymer chains plus counterions with Coulomb interactions between all charges, counterions were found to occupy sites between chains and produce effective chain–chain attraction (Orkoulas et al., 2003); this effect might be viewed as a primitive form of bridging.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orkoulas et al., 2003.

claim: Krainer et al., 2021's conclusion about reentrant salt effect was based on the salt dependences of the potentials of mean force calculated for pairs of sidechains of various types.
source: Their conclusion was based on the salt dependences of the potentials of mean force calculated for pairs of sidechains of various types.
evidence: This describes the methodology used by Krainer et al., 2021.

claim: At high salt, the number of salt bridges remains constant while the numbers of π-types of interactions are elevated in the multi-chain system.
source: We show that, at high salt, the number of salt bridges remains constant while the numbers of π-types of interactions are elevated in the multi-chain system.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: High salt achieves the elevation of π-type interactions by drawing water away from π-interaction partners.
source: Our simulations further reveal that high salt achieves the latter effect by drawing water away from π-interaction partners.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are four distinct classes of salt dependence of homotypic phase separation: screening, reentrant, high net charge, and low net charge.
source: The present work puts us in a position to paint a unified picture of salt dependences of homotypic phase separation (Figure 6A, B and Table 1).
evidence: This is the classification scheme proposed based on the current understanding, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: In the screening class of salt dependence, salts weaken the electrostatic attraction between protein chains and thereby suppress phase separation.
source: The salt dependence that is most often reported is screening, where salts weaken the electrostatic attraction between protein chains and thereby suppress phase separation (Berry et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Brady et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2017; Reed and Hammer, 2018; Tsang et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The reentrant salt dependence can be seen as an extension of the screening scenario, whereby high salt overcompensates the screening effect by strengthening π-type and hydrophobic interactions and leads to reemergence of phase separation.
source: The reentrant salt dependence reported by Krainer et al., 2021 can be seen as an extension of the screening scenario, whereby high salt overcompensates the screening effect by strengthening π-type and hydrophobic interactions and leads to reemergence of phase separation.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of Krainer et al., 2021 and the current study.

claim: The high net charge scenario is similar to the reentrant scenario at high salt but differs from it at low salt, where phase separation is prevented by net charge repulsion.
source: The high net charge scenario represented by A1-LCD is similar to the reentrant scenario at high salt but differs from it at low salt, where phase separation is prevented by net charge repulsion (Martin et al., 2021; Muschol and Rosenberger, 1997; Kim et al., 2017; Dao et al., 2018; Babinchak et al., 2019; Le Ferrand et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2021; Otis and Sharpe, 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the current study and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the high net charge class of salt dependence, a certain amount of salt is required to start phase separation.
source: In this class of salt dependence, a certain amount of salt is required to start phase separation.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of A1-LCD and other proteins in this class.

claim: For A1-LCD, the minimum salt required to start phase separation is ~100 mM NaCl.
source: For A1-LCD, this minimum salt is ~100 mM NaCl (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: RMFP-1 has a net charge of +24 over a sequence length of 121 and requires up to 700 mM NaCl to begin phase separation.
source: The recombinant mussel foot protein-1 (RMFP-1) presents an extreme example, which has a net charge of +24 over a sequence length of 121 and requires up to 700 mM NaCl to begin phase separation (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: The fourth class of salt dependence (low net charge) is a variation of the high net charge class; here, the net charge is low and no significant net charge repulsion is expected, so the protein can phase separate even without salt.
source: The fourth class of salt dependence is a variation of the preceding one; here, the net charge is low and no significant net charge repulsion is expected, so the protein can phase separate even without salt.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of proteins in this class.

claim: FUS-LCD has a low net charge of −2 and phase separates without salt.
source: For example, FUS-LCD has a low net charge of −2 and phase separates without salt (Burke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burke et al., 2015.

claim: At pH 7, TDP43-LCD has a relatively low net charge of +5 and phase separates without salt; the salt dependence thus belongs to the low net charge class.
source: At pH 7, this protein has a relatively low net charge of +5 and phase separates without salt; the salt dependence thus belongs to the low net charge class.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Babinchak et al., 2019.

claim: When pH is lowered to 4, TDP43-LCD's net charge increases to +11; now phase separation requires 300 mM NaCl and the salt dependence switches to the high net charge class.
source: When pH is lowered to 4, the six His residues in the purification tag become positively charged, raising the net charge to +11; now phase separation requires 300 mM NaCl and the salt dependence switches to the high net charge class.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Babinchak et al., 2019.

claim: Three determinants of salt dependence class are: (1) the total number of charged residues, (2) the net charge, and (3) the total number of aromatic residues.
source: The foregoing physical understanding suggests three determinants of salt dependence class: (1) the total number of charged residues, which determines the contribution of electrostatic interactions to the drive for phase separation and the importance of salt screening; (2) the net charge, which determines the magnitude of net charge repulsion; and (3) the total number of aromatic residues, which determines whether phase separation reemerges at high salt.
evidence: This is inferred from the physical understanding developed in the study.

claim: The screening class occurs when the charged content is high but the net charge and aromatic content are low.
source: We predict that the screening class occurs when the charged content is high but the net charge and aromatic content are low (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the physical understanding and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: For the reentrant class, the increase in aromatic content is the only difference from the screening class.
source: For the reentrant class, the increase in aromatic content is the only difference from the screening class.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the physical understanding and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: For the high net charge class, the net charge has to be high, but that could also mean at least a moderately high charged content.
source: For the high net charge class, the net charge obviously has to be high, but that could also mean at least a moderately high charged content.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the physical understanding and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: The low net charge class is predicted when the net charge is low but no bias is required of the charged content.
source: Finally, the low net charge class is predicted when the net charge is low but no bias is required of the charged content.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the physical understanding and illustrated in Figure 6C.

claim: Of the 17 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a high aromatic content, 12 (or 71%) actually have this feature (aromatic content >8% threshold).
source: For example, of the 17 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a high aromatic content, 12 (or 71%) actually have this feature (aromatic content >an 8% threshold).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Of the 10 proteins in the screening class of salt dependence that calls for a low aromatic content, only 2 (or 20%) have an aromatic content above the 8% threshold.
source: In contrast, of the 10 proteins in the class of salt dependence (i.e., 'screening') that calls for a low aromatic content, only 2 (or 20%) have an aromatic content above the threshold.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Of the 10 proteins in the high net charge class that calls for a high net charge, 7 (or 70%) actually have this feature (net charge >6% threshold).
source: Likewise, of the 10 proteins in the class of salt dependence (i.e., 'high net charge') that calls for a high net charge, 7 (or 70%) actually have this feature (net charge >a 6% threshold).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Of the 17 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a low net charge, none has a net charge above the 6% threshold.
source: In contrast, of the 17 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a low net charge, none has a net charge above the threshold.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Of the 15 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a high charge content, 11 (or 73%) actually have this feature (charged content >20% threshold).
source: Lastly, of the 15 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that call for a high charge content, 11 (or 73%) actually have this feature (charged content >a 20% threshold).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Of the 12 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that do not require a high charge content, only 2 (or 17%) have a charge content above the 20% threshold.
source: In comparison, of the 12 proteins in the classes of salt dependence that do not require a high charge content, only 2 (or 17%) have a charge content above the threshold.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 1.

claim: Caprin1's phase separation required 500 mM NaCl and was promoted by higher salt, behaving as if in the high net charge class of salt dependence.
source: Caprin1's phase separation required 500 mM NaCl and was promoted by higher salt (Wong et al., 2020), and thus behaved as if in the high net charge class of salt dependence (Figure 6A, third panel).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wong et al., 2020.

claim: pY-Caprin1's phase separation was suppressed by salt, behaving as if in the screening class.
source: In contrast, pY-Caprin1's phase separation was suppressed by salt (Lin et al., 2024), behaving as if in the screening class (Figure 6A, first panel).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: The amino-acid composition-based predictor correctly places both Caprin1 and pY-Caprin1 in their respective salt dependence classes.
source: Our amino-acid composition-based predictor correctly places both proteins in these respective classes (Table 1), with Caprin1's sequence possessing both a high net charge and a high aromatic content whereas pY-Caprin1's sequence possessing a high level of charged residues.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The disparate salt dependences of Caprin1 and pY-Caprin1 were correctly captured by both analytical theory and coarse-grained simulations.
source: The disparate salt dependences of these two proteins were also correctly captured by both analytical theory and coarse-grained simulations (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2024.

claim: Coarse-grained simulations of Caprin1 showed the dominance of Cl– over Na+ in partitioning into the dense phase, similar to all-atom simulations of A1-LCD.
source: The simulations also showed the dominance of Cl– over Na+ in partitioning into the dense phase of Caprin1, similar to our all-atom simulations of A1-LCD (Figure 3B); both Caprin1 and A1-LCD have a high net positive charge.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2024 and comparison to the current study's data.

claim: Coarse-grained simulations can readily capture the phase-separation process and represent the equilibrium between the dense and dilute phases.
source: Coarse-grained simulations can readily capture the phase-separation process and represent the equilibrium between the dense and dilute phases.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of coarse-grained simulations.

claim: For short peptides, all-atom simulations have been shown to accomplish both capturing the phase-separation process and representing the equilibrium between phases.
source: For short peptides, all-atom simulations have been shown to accomplish both of these tasks (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: For the mixture of ATP and a 33-residue IDP, all-atom simulations were able to capture the condensation process but not the equilibration of the resulting dense phase with a dilute phase.
source: For the mixture of ATP and a 33-residue IDP, all-atom simulations were able to capture the condensation process but not the equilibration of the resulting dense phase with a dilute phase (Kota et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kota et al., 2024.

claim: The number of protein chains (8) in the A1-LCD simulations is too low for a proper representation of a homogenous solution at low salt and a full equilibration between two phases at intermediate and high salt.
source: In this work, although the total number of atoms in the A1-LCD system, ~half a million, is very high from a computational standpoint, the number of protein chains (i.e., 8) is still too low for a proper representation of a homogenous solution at low salt and a full equilibration between two phases at intermediate and high salt.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the simulation setup.

claim: The A1-LCD simulations do not show condensation at low salt, thus mimicking a homogenous solution.
source: Nevertheless, our simulations do not show condensation at low salt, thus mimicking a homogenous solution
evidence: This is observed in the simulation data (Figure 1C, Figure 2A).

claim: The A1-LCD simulations at intermediate and high salt show condensation and thus model the dense phase.
source: the simulations at intermediate and high salt show condensation and thus model the dense phase.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation data (Figure 1D, Figure 2A).

claim: The all-atom simulations are able to capture unusual physical effects that could be missed in coarse-grained simulations, such as strengthening π-types of interactions by drawing water away from the interaction partners.
source: Importantly, the all-atom simulations are able to capture unusual physical effects that could be missed in coarse-grained simulations, such as strengthening π-types of interactions by drawing water away from the interaction partners.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the water RDF analysis in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of strengthening π-types of interactions by drawing water away from interaction partners is now confirmed by Raman spectroscopy.
source: The latter effect is now confirmed by Raman spectroscopy (Joshi et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2024.

claim: Salts regulate intermolecular interactions in biomolecular condensates in a variety of ways, but the net dependence of homotypic phase separation on salt concentration can be placed into four distinct classes.
source: To conclude, salts regulate intermolecular interactions in biomolecular condensates in a variety of ways, but the net dependence of homotypic phase separation on salt concentration can be placed into four distinct classes (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, illustrated in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The four classes of salt dependence are predictable from the protein amino-acid composition.
source: Moreover, these classes are predictable from the protein amino-acid composition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figure 6C and Table 1.

claim: Salts exert significant effects on heterotypic condensates.
source: Salts also exert significant effects on heterotypic condensates (Farag et al., 2023; Galvanetto et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The conclusions drawn on homotypic condensates may prove instructive for heterotypic condensates.
source: the conclusions drawn here on homotypic condensates may prove instructive for heterotypic condensates.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential applicability of the findings.

claim: A fluctuation in intracellular salt concentration may promote the phase separation of some IDPs and suppress the phase separation of other IDPs.
source: For example, a fluctuation in intracellular salt concentration may promote the phase separation of some IDPs and suppress the phase separation of other IDPs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological implications.

claim: If two IDPs co-phase separate or form heterotypic condensates, salt fluctuations may change the protein composition of condensates and the relative contributions of the individual proteins to phase separation.
source: If two IDPs co-phase separate or form heterotypic condensates, salt fluctuations may change the protein composition of condensates and the relative contributions of the individual proteins to phase separation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential biological implications.

claim: The atomistic details of ion coordination to A1-LCD backbone or sidechain groups are reminiscent of those observed in channels and transporters for Na+ and Cl–.
source: Lastly, we note that the atomistic details of ion coordination to A1-LCD backbone or sidechain groups are reminiscent of those observed in other systems, in particular channels and transporters for Na+ and Cl– (Mancusso et al., 2012; Mita et al., 2021; Leisle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.
